## Overview

Three sessions this week:

1. **Tutorial 1** - Generating and plotting single realisations
2. **Tutorial 2** - Many realisations: spaghetti and small multiples
3. **Tutorial 3** - Summarising ensembles with ribbons, and a short written comparison exercise

This document gives one worked solution for each exercise. Answers to
open-ended questions are one reasonable response, not the only correct
one — the R/ggplot2 code and the reasoning behind it are the important
part.

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)
```

---

## Tutorial 1: Generating and plotting single realisations

### 1.1 A random walk

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
n <- 100

walk_df <- data.frame(
  time = 1:n,
  position = cumsum(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1))
)

head(walk_df)
set.seed(2026)
head(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1))

ggplot(walk_df, aes(time, position)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Random walk, sd = 1",
       x = "Step", y = "Position") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 1.1 - Solution**

Seeds used: `sd = 0.5` -> seed `2027`; `sd = 1` -> seed `2026`
(as above); `sd = 2` -> seed `2028`. Recording the seed for each
series is what makes the figure reproducible even though three
different random draws went into it.

```{r}
set.seed(2027)
walk_05 <- data.frame(time = 1:n,
                       position = cumsum(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 0.5)),
                       sd = "0.5")

set.seed(2026)
walk_1 <- data.frame(time = 1:n,
                      position = cumsum(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)),
                      sd = "1")

set.seed(2028)
walk_2 <- data.frame(time = 1:n,
                      position = cumsum(rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 2)),
                      sd = "2")

walks_all <- bind_rows(walk_05, walk_1, walk_2)

ggplot(walks_all, aes(time, position, colour = sd)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Random walks for sd = 0.5, 1, 2",
       x = "Step", y = "Position", colour = "sd") +
  theme_minimal()
```

*What happens to the y-axis range?* The spread of the walk grows with
`sd`, and it grows faster than linearly with the number of steps: for
a simple random walk the standard deviation of the position at step
`t` is `sd * sqrt(t)`. Doubling `sd` roughly doubles the y-axis range
needed, and the `sd = 2` series visually dwarfs the `sd = 0.5` series
even though both start at the same point.

### 1.2 Faceting by parameter

**Exercise 1.2 - Solution**

The seed is set once, before generating all six series, so the six
draws are six genuinely different segments of the same random stream
rather than six copies of the same numbers (which is what would happen
if the seed were reset inside the loop). That keeps the panels
independent and comparable, and keeps the whole figure reproducible
from a single seed.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)

params <- expand.grid(sd = c(0.5, 1, 2), drift = c(0, 0.1))

facet_df <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(params)), function(i) {
  sd_i    <- params$sd[i]
  drift_i <- params$drift[i]
  data.frame(
    time = 1:n,
    position = cumsum(rnorm(n, mean = drift_i, sd = sd_i)),
    sd = sd_i,
    drift = drift_i
  )
})
facet_df <- bind_rows(facet_df)

ggplot(facet_df, aes(time, position)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_grid(sd ~ drift,
             labeller = label_bquote(rows = sd == .(sd),
                                      cols = drift == .(drift))) +
  labs(title = "Random walks across sd (rows) and drift (columns)",
       x = "Step", y = "Position") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Tutorial 2: Many realisations - spaghetti and small multiples

### 2.1 Generating an ensemble

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
n_steps <- 100
n_sims  <- 50

sims <- lapply(1:n_sims, function(i) {
  data.frame(sim = i, time = 1:n_steps,
             position = cumsum(rnorm(n_steps)))
})
sims <- bind_rows(sims)
```

### 2.2 Spaghetti plot

Trying different alphas: (to anticipate the next question)

```{r}
ggplot(sims, aes(time, position, group = sim)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 1, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "50 random walk realisations - alpha = 1") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(sims, aes(time, position, group = sim)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "50 random walk realisations - alpha = 0.3") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(sims, aes(time, position, group = sim)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "50 random walk realisations - alpha = 0.15") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
ggplot(sims, aes(time, position, group = sim)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.05, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "50 random walk realisations - alpha = 0.05") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 2.1 - Solution**

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7
make_spaghetti <- function(n_sims, alpha_val, seed = 2026) {
  set.seed(seed)
  df <- lapply(1:n_sims, function(i) {
    data.frame(sim = i, time = 1:n_steps,
               position = cumsum(rnorm(n_steps)))
  })
  df <- bind_rows(df)

  ggplot(df, aes(time, position, group = sim)) +
    geom_line(alpha = alpha_val, colour = "steelblue") +
    labs(title = paste0("n = ", n_sims, ", alpha = ", alpha_val)) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9)
}

grid_params <- expand.grid(n_sims = c(50, 500), alpha_val = c(1, 0.3, 0.05))

plots <- Map(make_spaghetti, grid_params$n_sims, grid_params$alpha_val)

wrap_plots(plots, ncol = 3)
```

At `n = 50`, `alpha = 1` is already messy but individual paths are
still traceable; `alpha = 0.3` starts to reveal the density of the
bundle; `alpha = 0.05` is too faint and the ensemble almost
disappears because 50 lines don't build up enough overlap. At
`n = 500`, `alpha = 1` becomes a solid unreadable block, `alpha = 0.3`
is still too dense to separate paths, and `alpha = 0.05` is the first
setting where individual overplotting resolves into a readable density
gradient. In short: the useful alpha scales roughly like `1/n_sims`,
and a fixed alpha that works well for one `n` will usually fail badly
at another.

### 2.3 Small multiples

```{r}
sims |>
  filter(sim <= 9) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, position)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ sim, nrow = 3) +
  labs(title = "9 of 50 realisations") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Exercise 2.2 - Solution**

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8
sims |>
  filter(sim <= 25) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, position)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ sim, nrow = 5) +
  labs(title = "25 of 50 realisations") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)
```

Empirically, around 20-25 panels (a 5x5 grid) is about the practical
ceiling at a typical screen/slide size using `fig-width = 10`,
`fig-height = 8`: individual panel axes are still legible and shapes
are distinguishable. Beyond about 30 panels the per-panel plotting
area becomes too small to read axis labels, and by 50 panels the grid
is only useful for a very coarse "are these all roughly similar"
impression rather than for judging any individual trajectory.

### 2.4 Discussion (bring to class)

**Which representation better conveys...**

- **(a) the typical trajectory shape** - Small multiples, since each
  panel shows one full, uncluttered trajectory and the eye can trace
  its shape without interference from other lines.
- **(b) the spread of outcomes at the final time point** - The
  spaghetti plot, because overlapping semi-transparent lines let the
  eye read off density directly, and the vertical band of ink at the
  right-hand edge visually encodes the spread; a set of 9-25 small
  panels only samples a few final values and doesn't build up that
  density impression. (Tutorial 3's ribbon plot is a more precise way
  to answer this same question.)
- **(c) whether any individual trajectory is unusual** - Small
  multiples again: an unusual path is easy to spot in its own panel,
  but in a spaghetti plot with many overlapping lines a single unusual
  trajectory is often visually swamped by the rest of the bundle
  unless it is extreme.

**A process where small multiples would be preferable regardless of
`n`** - Any setting where the *shape over time* of an individual
series matters more than the ensemble's aggregate spread, and where
series are qualitatively different from one another rather than
exchangeable draws from the same process - for example, daily case
counts for different countries during an epidemic, or sensor traces
from different patients in an ICU. There, overlaying the series as
spaghetti would blur exactly the between-series shape differences that
are the point of the plot, no matter how few or many series there are.

## Tutorial 3: Summarising ensembles

### 3.1 From realisations to summaries

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
n_steps <- 100
n_sims  <- 500

sims_big <- lapply(1:n_sims, function(i) {
  data.frame(sim = i, time = 1:n_steps,
             position = cumsum(rnorm(n_steps)))
})
sims_big <- bind_rows(sims_big)

summary_df <- sims_big |>
  group_by(time) |>
  summarise(
    median  = median(position),
    lower50 = quantile(position, 0.25),
    upper50 = quantile(position, 0.75),
    lower90 = quantile(position, 0.05),
    upper90 = quantile(position, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

**Exercise 3.1 - Solution**

*Prediction*: the 90% band should get **wider** over time. Each step
adds an independent `rnorm()` increment, so the variance of the
position at time `t` is the sum of `t` independent variances and grows
linearly in `t` (variance = `t * sd^2`); the standard deviation, and
hence the width of any fixed-probability interval, grows like
`sqrt(t)`. There's no drift to shift the band, only noise that
accumulates, so uncertainty about "where am I now" necessarily
increases the longer the walk has been running.

### 3.2 Ribbon plots and comparison

```{r}
ggplot(summary_df, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower90, ymax = upper90),
              alpha = 0.2, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower50, ymax = upper50),
              alpha = 0.4, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Random walk: median, 50% and 90% intervals (500 sims)",
       x = "Time", y = "Position") +
  theme_minimal()
```

This confirms the prediction from Exercise 3.1: both the 50% and 90%
bands visibly widen as `time` increases, consistent with variance
growing linearly in the number of steps.

**Exercise 3.2 - Solution**

```{r}
set.seed(1)
sample_sims <- sample(unique(sims_big$sim), 10)

sample_df <- sims_big |> filter(sim %in% sample_sims)

# Version A: ribbon only
p_ribbon_only <- ggplot(summary_df, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower90, ymax = upper90),
              alpha = 0.2, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower50, ymax = upper50),
              alpha = 0.4, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Ribbon only") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

# Version B: ribbon + 10 sampled trajectories
p_ribbon_lines <- ggplot(summary_df, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower90, ymax = upper90),
              alpha = 0.2, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lower50, ymax = upper50),
              alpha = 0.4, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(data = sample_df, aes(y = position, group = sim),
            colour = "grey30", alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = median), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Ribbon + 10 sampled trajectories") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9)

# notice that adding `colour = as.factor(sim)` in the `geom_line(data = sample_df...`
# aes() gets different colours for the individual trajectories. Maybe better to 
# get fewer than 10 then. 5 is good and makes them clearly identifiable.

p_ribbon_only + p_ribbon_lines
```

*Chosen version and justification*: Version B (ribbon plus a handful
of individual trajectories) communicates better here. The ribbon alone
answers "how much spread is there" but hides that individual paths are
often much rougher than the smooth median line suggests; adding just
10 thin, low-alpha trajectories grounds the abstract interval in
concrete example paths without seriously cluttering the plot, since 10
lines at low alpha stay visually subordinate to the ribbon. Adding all
500 trajectories, by contrast, would clutter the plot and defeat the
purpose of summarising in the first place - the value of the small
sample is that it illustrates without overwhelming.

> **Looking ahead**: keep your ensemble data frame (or the code that
> generates it). Week 6's tutorials will revisit the ribbon idea, but
> applied to *model-based* intervals (confidence/prediction intervals,
> bootstrap distributions) rather than simulation ensembles. The visual
> grammar is the same; the source of the uncertainty differs.
